disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), Combined Presentation, is characterized by a persistent pattern of both inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity that interferes with functioning across settings (e.g., work, school, home) and begins in childhood, though it may not be formally recognized until later in life. Adults typically present with difficulties in sustained focus, organization, and follow-through, alongside inner restlessness or impulsive behaviors, rather than the overt motor hyperactivity more typical in children. The course is usually chronic, with symptoms waxing and waning depending on environmental demands, stress, and structure, and it is distinct from mood, anxiety, or personality disorders by its early onset, trait-like pattern, and specific cognitive/behavioral profile. Comorbid anxiety, depression, or substance use are common, and functional impairment—rather than the mere presence of symptoms—is central to diagnosis.

narrative.stressor: Over the past two years, Josue’s company shifted from longer, project-based tickets to a high-volume, rapid-response support model with strict metrics for call times, documentation accuracy, and simultaneous queue management. The constant context-switching and need to track multiple complex issues at once began to clash with his usual style of deep-focus troubleshooting and late-night tinkering, leading to missed follow-ups, overlooked details in change tickets, and tension with a new metrics-driven manager. At the same time, he started informally mentoring junior staff and taking evening courses to prepare for a management role, further increasing demands on his planning and organizational capacities. When a critical misconfiguration he overlooked during a busy shift caused network downtime for a major client and led to a formal performance improvement plan, he was urged by his supervisor—who suspected an underlying attention issue—to seek a psychiatric evaluation, which is when his long-standing but now clearly impairing difficulties came to clinical attention.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep losing track of what I’m supposed to be working on and can’t seem to stay organized with all the tickets and follow-ups at my job.”

narrative.stressor: As Tracey transitioned further into retirement and took on a larger volunteer role designing intergenerational programs at the community center, the loss of her long-standing household manager structure exposed long-compensated attention difficulties. Her days became packed with dance classes, book club, travel planning, cooking for large potlucks, and coordinating volunteers, but without the external routines of full-time work, she found it increasingly hard to keep track of schedules, materials, and small but important tasks. Misplacing knitting supplies and recipe notes, double-booking events, and forgetting to complete key errands for community programs began to frustrate both her and her collaborators, leading her husband and friends to worry that she might be developing early dementia. Concerned by these changes yet aware that her memory for conversations and stories seemed intact, she agreed to see a psychiatrist after her primary care physician suggested that a long-standing attention disorder, rather than primary neurocognitive decline, might explain her recent functional struggles.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m constantly forgetting little everyday things—appointments, errands, even finishing what I start for the community center.”

narrative.stressor: Leandro left a series of entry-level jobs at garages and parts stores over the past two years because he struggled to keep up with the fast pace, multi-step service orders, and certification study requirements, despite his genuine interest and hands-on talent with cars. As bills mounted and he moved back in with his parents, family pressure to contribute financially increased, and his careful budgeting couldn’t compensate for his difficulty following through on applications, training programs, and side gigs he tried to start. His inability to translate his detailed plans into consistent action—missing appointment times, losing track of paperwork, and getting sidetracked while studying—left him feeling stuck and ashamed, especially as cousins his age advanced in their own careers. After he forgot about an important intake appointment for an automotive training program he had waited months for, his older sister, who had been diagnosed with ADHD herself, urged him to get evaluated, and he agreed when he realized his long-standing attention problems were now directly threatening his financial independence and career goals.
narrative.chief_complaint: “No matter how interested I am, I can’t keep my attention on job training or applications long enough to finish them.”
